clauses.heading: Insurance
clauses.contentText:
Insurance
The Supplier shall maintain, with a reputable insurer, professional indemnity insurance of at least £10,000,000, cyber liability insurance of at least £10,000,000, public liability insurance of at least £5,000,000 and employer's liability insurance of at least £5,000,000.
The Supplier shall provide certificates of insurance to the Customer on request, and shall notify the Customer if any policy is cancelled or materially reduced.
The Supplier's insurance shall respond to claims covered by it in accordance with its terms, but the existence of insurance does not increase or otherwise affect the limitations in Clause 11.

clauses.heading: Term and termination
clauses.contentText:
Term and termination
This Agreement begins on the Effective Date and continues for three (3) years, unless terminated earlier in accordance with this Clause 13.
At the end of the initial term, this Agreement shall automatically renew for successive periods of twelve (12) months unless either party gives written notice at least one hundred and twenty (120) days before the end of the then-current term.
Either party may terminate this Agreement with immediate effect by written notice if the other party commits a material breach and fails to remedy it within thirty (30) days of written notice.
Either party may terminate this Agreement with immediate effect by written notice if the other party becomes insolvent, enters administration, has a receiver appointed, or ceases to carry on business.
The Supplier may suspend the Services if the Customer fails to pay undisputed Fees in accordance with Clause 4, or if suspension is necessary to prevent a security incident or unlawful use.
Termination of this Agreement does not affect any accrued rights or liabilities of either party, and the provisions that by their nature should survive termination shall survive, including Clauses 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 14, 17, 18 and 19.
On termination, the Customer shall pay all Fees accrued to the effective date of termination. The Supplier shall provide the exit assistance described in Schedule 1 for ninety (90) days at its standard rates.

clauses.heading: Audit and records
clauses.contentText:
Audit and records
The Supplier shall maintain complete and accurate records of its provision of the Services and its compliance with this Agreement for a period of six (6) years after the end of the year to which the records relate.
The Customer may, on at least five (5) Business Days' prior written notice and no more than twice in any twelve-month period, audit Supplier's compliance with this Agreement, including access to Supplier's personnel, systems and sub-processors.
The audit shall be conducted during normal business hours, remotely where possible, and shall not interfere with the Supplier's operations or compromise the security or confidentiality of other customers' data.
The auditor shall be independent, bound by confidentiality obligations at least as protective as Clause 7, and shall not have access to the Supplier's source code or to any other customer's data.
The Customer shall bear the cost of the audit unless the audit reveals a material discrepancy of more than five per cent (5%) in the Fees or a material breach of Schedule 2.

clauses.heading: Subcontracting
clauses.contentText:
Subcontracting
The Supplier may subcontract any part of the Services to its Affiliates or to third parties, provided that it remains responsible for the performance of the subcontracted Services and imposes obligations on the subcontractor that are consistent with this Agreement.
The Supplier shall list its sub-processors in Schedule 4 and shall notify the Customer of any change in accordance with that Schedule.
The Supplier shall not subcontract the provision of the Platform to a direct competitor of the Customer without the Customer's prior written consent.
Any subcontracting does not relieve the Supplier of its obligations under this Agreement.

clauses.heading: Force majeure
clauses.contentText:
Force majeure
A party is not liable for any failure or delay in performing its obligations under this Agreement to the extent caused by a Force Majeure Event, provided that it notifies the other party promptly and uses reasonable endeavours to mitigate the effect.
A Force Majeure Event does not excuse the Customer from paying Fees for Services already provided.
If a Force Majeure Event continues for more than sixty (60) days, either party may terminate the affected Order Form or SOW on written notice without liability, except for Fees accrued to the date of termination.

clauses.heading: Notices
clauses.contentText:
Notices
Notices under this Agreement must be in writing and delivered by hand or by recorded post to the addresses set out below, with a copy to the recipient's legal department.
Notices to the Customer shall be sent to Kestrel Assurance Group plc, 1 Waterhouse Quay, Leeds LS1 4BR, for the attention of the General Counsel, with a copy to the Head of Procurement.
Notices to the Supplier shall be sent to Bramber Software Limited, The Glass Works, 12 Feeder Road, Bristol BS2 0SB, for the attention of the General Counsel.
A notice is deemed received on delivery, if delivered by hand, or two Business Days after posting, if sent by recorded post.

clauses.heading: Governing law and disputes
clauses.contentText:
Governing law and disputes
This Agreement and any dispute arising out of or in connection with it are governed by the laws of England and Wales.
The parties submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of England and Wales sitting in Leeds.
Before commencing proceedings, the parties shall escalate the dispute to their respective senior representatives, who shall meet within ten (10) Business Days and attempt in good faith to resolve it for a further twenty (20) Business Days.
Nothing in this Clause prevents either party from applying for injunctive relief or other urgent relief at any time.

clauses.heading: General
clauses.contentText:
General
This Agreement, together with the Order Forms, SOWs and Schedules, constitutes the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior discussions, proposals and representations, except for fraudulent misrepresentation.
No variation of this Agreement is effective unless made in writing and signed by authorised representatives of both parties.
Neither party may assign this Agreement without the other's prior written consent, except to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger or sale of substantially all of its assets, provided that the assignee assumes the assigning party's obligations in writing.
No failure or delay in exercising a right operates as a waiver of that right, and no single exercise prevents any further exercise.
If any provision of this Agreement is found to be invalid or unenforceable, the remaining provisions shall continue in full force and effect, and the parties shall negotiate a valid replacement that achieves the original commercial intent.
A person who is not a party to this Agreement has no right under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 to enforce any provision of it.
Neither party shall use the other's name, logo or trademarks in any press release, advertisement, case study or public communication without the other's prior written consent, except that the Supplier may include the Customer's name in a confidential list of reference customers provided to prospective customers under a written confidentiality obligation.
Each party shall comply with all applicable anti-bribery, anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, and shall not offer or accept any bribe or improper payment in connection with this Agreement.
The parties shall comply with all applicable export control and sanctions laws in relation to the Services and Customer Data.
This Agreement may be executed in counterparts, each of which is an original and all of which together constitute one instrument.
The headings in this Agreement are for convenience only and do not affect its interpretation.

clauses.heading: Support priorities
clauses.contentText:
Support priorities
A Priority 1 incident is a complete loss of the production Platform or a security incident affecting Customer Data. A Priority 2 incident is a material impairment of a core function with no workaround. A Priority 3 incident is a minor defect or a question about the Documentation.

ISO/IEC 27001 certification and a SOC 2 Type II report, renewed annually.

Inventory of systems and data assets, with ownership and classification assigned.

between
VANTAGE HEALTH GMBH
and
BRAMBER SOFTWARE LIMITED
Dated: 3 March 2026
This Data Processing Agreement is made on 3 March 2026 between:
(1) VANTAGE HEALTH GMBH, a company incorporated in Germany with registration number HRB 214887, whose registered office is at Ridlerstraße 31, 80339 München, Germany (the “Controller”); and

(2) BRAMBER SOFTWARE LIMITED, a private limited company incorporated in England and Wales with company number 08841267, whose registered office is at The Glass Works, 12 Feeder Road, Bristol BS2 0SB (the “Processor”).
Background

(A) The Controller provides health insurance and care management services in Germany and uses the Processor's Bramber Flow platform for claims triage and case management under a master services agreement dated 14 January 2026 (the “MSA”).
(B) The processing of Personal Data under the MSA is subject to the requirements of Article 28 of the EU GDPR and, where applicable, the UK GDPR.
(C) The parties wish to set out the terms on which the Processor processes Personal Data on behalf of the Controller.

(D) The Controller has determined that the processing requires a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of the EU GDPR. The Processor has provided the information in Schedules 1 and 3 for that assessment.
The parties agree as follows:
Definitions and interpretation
In this Agreement, the following terms have the following meanings:

Affiliate means any entity that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with a party, where control means the ownership of more than fifty per cent (50%) of the voting shares or the ability to direct management.
Agreement means this Data Processing Agreement, including its Schedules.
Business Day means a day other than a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday in England and Wales.
Data Subject means an identified or identifiable natural person to whom Personal Data relates.
EEA means the European Economic Area.
Effective Date means 1 April 2026.
Personal Data means any information relating to a Data Subject that the Processor processes on behalf of the Controller under the MSA.
Personal Data Breach means a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, Personal Data.
Processing means any operation performed on Personal Data, including collection, storage, retrieval, use, disclosure, deletion and destruction.

leaves.label: Parties and roles
leaves.definition: Identifies each legal entity and the role it holds, such as discloser or recipient, controller or processor, or licensor and licensee.

leaves.label: Definitions and interpretation
leaves.definition: Defines capitalised terms and sets rules for reading the agreement, such as headings, gender, and whether 'including' is exhaustive.

leaves.label: Effective date
leaves.definition: The date the agreement takes effect. It is not the signing date and not how long the agreement lasts.

leaves.label: Term
leaves.definition: How long the agreement lasts, from the start date to the end date. Not how long one particular duty lasts.

leaves.label: Renewal
leaves.definition: Automatic or optional extension of the term and the notice needed to stop it. Applies where the agreement has no fixed end.

leaves.label: Termination for cause
leaves.definition: Right to end the agreement early for material breach, insolvency or unlawful conduct, with any cure period. Also covers suspending service while a breach is uncured.

leaves.label: Termination for convenience
leaves.definition: Right for either party to end the agreement early without any cause, usually on written notice of a stated period and sometimes against a fee. Applies only where the agreement grants the right.

leaves.label: Suspension
leaves.definition: A right to pause the services or a party's performance for a time, for example for unpaid fees or a security risk, without ending the agreement.

leaves.label: Survival
leaves.definition: Names the clauses that keep operating after the agreement ends, and for how long. Not the length of the agreement itself.

leaves.label: Confidential information scope
leaves.definition: What counts as confidential information, including oral or marked disclosures, and the exclusions for public, already known, independently developed and third-party sourced material.

leaves.label: Confidentiality obligations
leaves.definition: The receiving party's duties: use the information only as allowed, protect it to at least reasonable care, and tell the discloser if it is lost or disclosed.

leaves.label: Permitted purpose
leaves.definition: Limits the use of confidential information to a stated purpose, such as evaluating a transaction, and bans every other use.

leaves.label: Disclosure to representatives
leaves.definition: Who else may see the information, such as employees, advisers, affiliates and financing sources, the conditions attached, and who is responsible for their acts.

leaves.label: Compelled disclosure
leaves.definition: Permission to disclose where a court, regulator or law requires it, including a foreign government's demand for data held overseas, with notice to the other party. Not the governing law clause.

leaves.label: Residuals
leaves.definition: A right to use confidential information that staff happen to retain in unaided memory, despite the use and confidentiality duties.

leaves.label: Confidentiality period
leaves.definition: How long the confidentiality duty lasts after disclosure or termination, including any longer or indefinite period for trade secrets. Not the agreement's own length.

leaves.label: Return or destruction
leaves.definition: On exit, returning, deleting or destroying confidential material or personal data, including copies and backups, subject to a retention exception. In a DPA the controller chooses.

leaves.label: No commitment
leaves.definition: States that disclosure creates no obligation to do a deal, grants no licence and makes no representation. Not the warranty disclaimer, and not a positive grant of rights, which is LICENSE_GRANT.

leaves.label: Details of processing
leaves.definition: The subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of the processing, the types of personal data and the categories of data subjects, usually set out in a table.

leaves.label: Processor duties
leaves.definition: What the processor must do: follow documented instructions, keep the data confidential, not use it for its own purposes, and pass the terms to its personnel.

leaves.label: Controller obligations
leaves.definition: What the controller must do for the arrangement: hold the rights and a lawful basis in the data, give clear instructions, supply the data, and tell the processor if the processing changes.

leaves.label: Security measures
leaves.definition: The technical and organisational safeguards the provider must keep, such as encryption and access control, any named certification like SOC 2, and business continuity, backup and disaster recovery with recovery time and point objectives.

leaves.label: Breach notification
leaves.definition: Duty to tell the controller or customer quickly after a security or personal data incident, what the notice must contain, and who pays for it.

leaves.label: Sub-processors
leaves.definition: Whether the processor may appoint other processors, how authorisation works, notice of changes and objection rights, and flow-down of the same duties.

leaves.label: Data subject and regulatory assistance
leaves.definition: Processor help with data subject rights requests, regulator enquiries, impact assessments and breach consultations, usually charged at agreed rates.

leaves.label: International transfers
leaves.definition: The conditions and legal mechanism for sending personal data outside its origin country, such as the EU or UK standard contractual clauses, and any transfer risk assessment.

leaves.label: Customer data ownership and use
leaves.definition: Who owns customer data and what the provider may do with it, including aggregation, de-identification and service analytics. Anything naming training, a model or machine learning is AI_AND_MODEL_TRAINING.

leaves.label: AI and model training
leaves.definition: Whether the provider may use customer data, inputs, prompts or outputs to train, fine-tune or improve any AI or machine-learning model, and whether the customer can opt out. Applies to personal data or not.

leaves.label: Fees and payment
leaves.definition: Prices, invoicing, payment deadlines, late-payment interest, expenses, price rises during the term, discounts, how usage is metered and disputed, and overage above the committed volume. Not a promise about other customers, which is MOST_FAVORED_NATION.

leaves.label: Volume commitments
leaves.definition: Minimum purchase, spend or metered usage a customer commits to, tiered price steps, and true-up at the end of the term. Not seat, user or site caps, which are LICENSE_RESTRICTIONS.

leaves.label: Taxes
leaves.definition: Which party bears which taxes, withholding on payments, and whether the payer must gross up.

leaves.label: Exclusivity
leaves.definition: Rights granted to one party on an exclusive basis, or limits on dealing with competitors, including any carve-outs.

leaves.label: Most favoured nation
leaves.definition: A promise that pricing and terms are no less favourable than those given to other customers or partners.

leaves.label: Right of first refusal or offer
leaves.definition: A right to be offered, or to match, a proposed sale, licence or transfer before it goes to a third party.

leaves.label: Standing and negotiation obligations
leaves.definition: Obligations to stay in discussions: negotiate in good faith, negotiate exclusively for a period, or pay a break fee if the deal ends. Not the statement that disclosure creates no obligation, which is NO_COMMITMENT.

leaves.label: Scope and deliverables
leaves.definition: What the provider must deliver: services, deliverables, milestones and dates, assumptions and exclusions, plus what the customer must supply in return.

leaves.label: Acceptance
leaves.definition: How a deliverable is accepted: review period, test criteria, deemed acceptance, reasons for rejection, cure, and any limit on the number of rejections.

leaves.label: Change control
leaves.definition: How scope, price or schedule changes are requested, approved, priced and recorded, and who may approve them.

leaves.label: Project governance
leaves.definition: Who decides what for the engagement: steering committee or working group, meeting cadence, escalation path and decision authority.

leaves.label: Service levels
leaves.definition: Measurable performance targets such as uptime or response times, how they are measured and reported, and remedies such as service credits and chronic failure.

leaves.label: Support and maintenance
leaves.definition: Support and maintenance after delivery: hours and channels, fixing defects, software updates and upgrades, and which version of the product is supported.

leaves.label: Subcontracting and personnel
leaves.definition: Whether the provider may use subcontractors, key person commitments and replacement rights, and responsibility for them. Not the same as sub-processors.

leaves.label: Transition assistance
leaves.definition: Help after termination to move the customer and its data elsewhere, including export format, duration, rates and any wind-down charges.

leaves.label: Feature deprecation and end of life
leaves.definition: Notice before a feature, version or service is withdrawn or end-of-lifed, roadmap and beta-feature commitments, and any right to refuse renewal or exit because of a deprecation. Not uptime targets or defect fixing.

leaves.label: Business continuity and disaster recovery
leaves.definition: Plans and duties to keep the services running, or restore them, after a serious disruption, such as backups, recovery time targets and continuity testing.

leaves.label: Assumptions and dependencies
leaves.definition: What the price and plan assume, and what the customer must provide or do, and what happens to time and cost if an assumption proves wrong.

leaves.label: IP ownership of work product
leaves.definition: Who owns new deliverables and work product, including any assignment of rights and what happens to jointly created material.

leaves.label: Pre-existing IP
leaves.definition: Each party keeps its own background or pre-existing IP, and any licence the other party needs to use it for the deliverables.

leaves.label: License grant
leaves.definition: The rights the licensor gives: which software or materials, how many copies or users, the delivery model, the term, and use by affiliates.

leaves.label: License restrictions
leaves.definition: Limits on use: no copying, reverse engineering, sublicensing or benchmarking beyond the licence, and caps by seat, user, site or field of use.

leaves.label: Perpetual or unlimited licence
leaves.definition: A licence that is perpetual or irrevocable, or unlimited in users, copies or usage, and whether it ever ends.

leaves.label: Source code escrow
leaves.definition: Deposit of source code or build materials with a third party, and the release events, update duty, verification and fees.

leaves.label: Third-party and open-source components
leaves.definition: Terms and obligations for bundled third-party and open-source software, including copyleft terms, and who is responsible for it.

leaves.label: Feedback licence
leaves.definition: A licence to use suggestions, ideas or feedback about the product or service, usually free of charge and royalty-free. Not the same as residuals.

leaves.label: Covenant not to sue
leaves.definition: A promise not to bring IP infringement claims against the other party for its own licensed or authorised use.

leaves.label: AI output rights
leaves.definition: Who owns or may use content the service generates from customer inputs, including prompts, completions and embeddings, and whether output is licensed or assigned. Not the provider's right to train models, which is AI_AND_MODEL_TRAINING.

leaves.label: Performance warranty
leaves.definition: A promise that the services or software conform to the specification or documentation and are performed with reasonable skill and care, and how long it lasts.

leaves.label: Non-infringement warranty
leaves.definition: A promise that using the software or deliverables as permitted will not infringe a third party's IP rights.

leaves.label: Representations and authority
leaves.definition: Statements of present fact at signing: authority to sign, due formation, no conflicting obligations, and no malicious code. Not an ongoing duty to comply with law.

leaves.label: Warranty disclaimer
leaves.definition: Excludes implied warranties and limits express ones to what the agreement says, often stating the information or service is provided as is.

leaves.label: Limitation of liability
leaves.definition: The ceiling on what each party can recover in total: the amount or formula, whether it is mutual, and what it covers.

leaves.label: Uncapped liability
leaves.definition: The claims that sit outside the cap, or under a higher super-cap, such as IP indemnity, data breach, confidentiality breach, gross negligence or wilful misconduct.

leaves.label: Exclusion of damages
leaves.definition: The waiver of indirect, consequential, special and punitive damages, usually also naming lost profit, lost revenue and loss of data.

leaves.label: Liquidated damages
leaves.definition: A fixed or agreed sum payable when a stated event happens, such as late delivery, instead of proving the actual loss. Not uptime service credits, which are SERVICE_LEVELS.

leaves.label: Indemnification
leaves.definition: A duty to defend and pay third-party claims for stated triggers, such as a data breach or property damage, with notice, defence control and settlement rules.

leaves.label: IP infringement indemnity
leaves.definition: The indemnity for third-party claims that the software or deliverables infringe IP, with its exclusions and its licence, replacement or refund remedy.

leaves.label: Insurance
leaves.definition: The types of insurance the provider must hold, the minimum limits, who pays, and evidence such as certificates.

leaves.label: Non-compete
leaves.definition: A restraint on competing with the other party in a stated market, territory or field for a stated period. Not a grant of exclusive rights, which is EXCLUSIVITY.

leaves.label: Non-solicitation of employees
leaves.definition: A restraint on soliciting or hiring the other party's employees or contractors for a stated period. Not a restraint on customers.

leaves.label: Non-solicitation of customers
leaves.definition: A restraint on soliciting or pursuing the other party's customers, clients or business partners for a stated period.

leaves.label: Non-disparagement
leaves.definition: A restraint on making negative public statements about the other party, its business or its products. Not the duty to keep information confidential, which is CONFIDENTIALITY_OBLIGATIONS.

leaves.label: Audit rights
leaves.definition: A right to inspect records or systems to check billing, licence use or compliance, with notice, frequency, cost and rules for the auditor.

leaves.label: Anti-corruption and trade compliance
leaves.definition: Obligations on bribery and corruption, sanctions, denied parties and export controls, including a right to end the agreement for breach.

leaves.label: Compliance with laws
leaves.definition: An ongoing duty to comply with laws and hold the permits and licences needed to perform, plus named standards such as WCAG accessibility or modern slavery reporting. Not a software licence grant.

leaves.label: Acceptable use
leaves.definition: The permitted use of a service and the banned activities, such as illegal content. Not seat, user or site caps, which are LICENSE_RESTRICTIONS. Suspension for breach is TERMINATION_FOR_CAUSE.

leaves.label: Governing law
leaves.definition: The legal system whose rules read the agreement. Not the courts, and not the duty to disclose where law requires it.

leaves.label: Jurisdiction and venue
leaves.definition: Which courts may hear a dispute, whether that choice is exclusive, and consent to bring proceedings there.

leaves.label: Dispute resolution
leaves.definition: The route for settling a dispute before or instead of court: escalation, mediation, arbitration rules and seat, and any jury trial waiver.

leaves.label: Equitable relief
leaves.definition: Whether a breach can be stopped by an injunction or specific performance without the injured party proving loss, including a clause that limits the remedies for a breach to damages.

leaves.label: Assignment
leaves.definition: Limits on transferring the agreement, whether consent is needed, and any permitted transfer to a successor, affiliate or purchaser.

leaves.label: Change of control
leaves.definition: Treats a sale of shares or other change in ownership as an assignment, or as a trigger for notice, consent or termination.

leaves.label: Notices
leaves.definition: How formal notices must be sent, to which address, and when a notice counts as received.

leaves.label: Force majeure
leaves.definition: Relief from performance when an event outside a party's control prevents it, with notice, mitigation and any right to end the agreement.

leaves.label: Publicity and marks
leaves.definition: Whether a party may use the other party's name, logo or trade marks in marketing, customer lists, press releases or case studies.

leaves.label: Third-party beneficiaries
leaves.definition: Whether people who are not parties, such as a party's affiliates or customers, may enforce rights under the agreement.

leaves.label: No agency or partnership
leaves.definition: States that the parties are independent, that neither can bind the other, and that nothing creates a partnership, agency or employment.

leaves.label: Miscellaneous boilerplate
leaves.definition: Counterparts, electronic signatures, headings and other reading aids, further assurance, and who bears its own legal costs. Not: entire agreement, severability, no agency or notices.

leaves.label: Entire agreement
leaves.definition: The agreement is the whole deal and replaces prior discussions, and any clause that cannot stand is severed without affecting the rest.

leaves.label: Amendment and waiver
leaves.definition: Changes must be in writing and signed, and a failure to enforce a right once is not a waiver of it.

leaves.label: Order of precedence
leaves.definition: Which document wins when the agreement, an order form, a statement of work, a data processing addendum or an online policy conflict.

data.text: Positions for customer DPAs where Bramber is the processor
UK GDPR; EU GDPR; UK IDTA and EU SCCs

This playbook sets out Bramber's position on data processing agreements where Bramber acts as a processor for a customer. It applies to customer DPAs, security schedules and the data protection terms in master services agreements. It does not cover situations where Bramber is a controller, such as marketing, HR or our own vendor relationships.

The regulatory backdrop is the UK GDPR and, for EU customers, the EU GDPR. The same positions work for both, with the transfer mechanism adjusted for the destination. Where a customer is a public authority or a regulated financial institution, additional sector rules may apply and the DPO must be involved before the first draft.

The positions below are written as preferred, fallback and walk-away. A fallback is pre-approved only where the processing is within the scope described in the DPA and no special category data is involved. Anything else goes to the DPO.
1.	Confirm the role allocation first. If the customer's DPA describes Bramber as a controller, stop and escalate: the entire document will need to be rewritten.

2.	Check the processing details in the schedule against the actual service. The schedule is the operative description of what we do; a generic schedule creates obligations we cannot map to our systems.
3.	Work through the positions in order. The first four determine whether the DPA is workable; the remainder are operational commitments that need an owner in the business.
4.	Record any fallback in the deal summary with the position ID. Do not agree a walk-away position in exchange for a commercial concession without the DPO and GC.
5.	Send the final DPA to the DPO for sign-off before signature. The DPO maintains the sub-processor list and the transfer register.

Each table below is one position. Read the Applies to row first; all twelve positions govern customer DPAs, including the data protection terms in a master services agreement.
Position IDs are stable and are used in deal summaries and approval requests. Quote the ID, not the heading, when you escalate.

Bramber is a processor and the customer is a controller. The DPA describes the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, the categories of personal data and the categories of data subjects in a schedule. Bramber does not determine the purposes or means of processing.

Bramber is a processor for customer data and an independent controller for account, billing and service telemetry data. The DPA must identify the controller data separately and limit the processor obligations to the customer data.
Any description of Bramber as a controller or joint controller of customer data, or any obligation to determine the lawful basis for the customer's processing.
Elena Marchetti, DPO. Priya Raghavan, GC for any controller or joint-controller language.

Role allocation is the foundation of the DPA. A processor acts on instructions; a controller decides why and how data is processed. Accepting controller language would make Bramber responsible for the customer's lawful basis, notices and retention decisions, which we cannot verify and do not control.

Bramber processes personal data only on the customer's documented instructions, including for transfers, unless required by law. If a law requires processing, Bramber informs the customer before processing unless prohibited from doing so. The DPA and the order form together constitute the instructions.
A general instruction to provide the services in accordance with the documentation, with a change-control process for new instructions and a right to charge for instruction changes.
An obligation to comply with instructions that are unlawful, or a right for the customer to instruct processing outside the scope of the services without a change order.

The instruction set is what separates a processor from a controller in practice. It also gives Bramber a defensible position if a customer asks for processing that is outside the documented service or unlawful in the destination country.

Personnel authorised to process personal data are bound by confidentiality obligations, have received appropriate training, and have access only on a need-to-know basis. Confidentiality survives termination of employment.
Confidentiality obligations in employment contracts plus annual privacy training, with evidence available on request rather than a separate undertaking for each engagement.
A requirement to name every individual with access, or to obtain customer approval for individual staff members.

Access control is an operational security measure, not a contractual permission slip. Naming individuals creates a maintenance burden and a privacy issue of its own; the customer needs assurance about the control, not the names.

The technical and organisational measures in the security schedule are appropriate to the risk and include encryption in transit and at rest, role-based access, logging and monitoring, vulnerability management, secure development, business continuity and incident response. Bramber maintains ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II.
The customer's security schedule where it is based on a recognised standard and does not require controls outside the current architecture. Any gap is recorded in a remediation plan with dates.
A requirement for controls Bramber does not operate, such as customer-held encryption keys without a managed service, on-premises deployment, or physical segregation of customer data.
Elena Marchetti, DPO. Jonas Reed, CISO for any control gap or remediation plan.

A security schedule is a statement of fact as well as a promise. Agreeing to a control we do not operate is a misrepresentation risk and creates an audit finding on day one. If the customer needs a control we do not have, price the change or decline the deal.
Prior written consent for new sub-processors, not unreasonably withheld or delayed, with deemed approval after 10 Business Days and a right to use affiliates without consent.
Absolute consent for each sub-processor, a veto over cloud infrastructure providers, or a requirement that Bramber's affiliates be treated as third parties requiring consent.
Elena Marchetti, DPO. Tom Whitlock, Senior Commercial Counsel for any consent right beyond general authorisation.

Our platform runs on hyperscale infrastructure and a small number of specialist services. A veto right over sub-processors is a veto over our ability to operate and scale. General authorisation with notice and objection is the model the EDPB guidelines contemplate for stable processing chains.

Transfers outside the UK or EEA are covered by the UK International Data Transfer Addendum, the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (Module 2) or an adequacy decision, together with a transfer risk assessment. The mechanism is named in the DPA and matches the destination.
The customer's preferred transfer mechanism where it is legally valid and the destination has been assessed. A supplementary measures schedule may be required for US transfers.
Transfers to a country without a valid mechanism, a representation that the destination is adequate when it is not, or an obligation to use a mechanism the customer has not executed.

A transfer clause is only as good as the mechanism behind it. The UK Addendum and the EU SCCs are the two mechanisms our customers most often require; naming the wrong one creates a gap that a regulator will find before we do.

Bramber assists the customer with data subject requests by appropriate technical and organisational measures, taking into account the nature of the processing. Assistance is provided within the customer's response window where feasible, and Bramber does not respond to requests directly unless instructed.
Assistance through the self-service tools in the platform, with bespoke support charged at standard professional services rates where the request requires manual work.
An obligation to respond directly to data subjects on the customer's behalf, or to guarantee a response within a period shorter than the platform's deletion and export cycles allow.

The customer owns the relationship with the data subject. Our obligation is to give them the tools and information they need, not to become the controller's front office. A direct-response obligation also creates a risk of conflicting instructions from different customers.

Bramber notifies the customer without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach affecting customer data. The notice includes the nature of the breach, the data and individuals affected, likely consequences and measures taken or proposed.

Notification within 72 hours of awareness, with an initial notice followed by a fuller report within 5 Business Days. A 72-hour period is the regulatory outer limit for the controller, not a target for the processor.
Notification within 5 Business Days or more, a requirement to notify the regulator directly on the customer's behalf, or an obligation to indemnify the customer for all regulatory fines.
Elena Marchetti, DPO. Jonas Reed, CISO for any change to the notification period.

The controller's 72-hour clock starts when it becomes aware, which is usually when we tell it. A processor notification period that consumes the whole 72 hours leaves the customer unable to comply. Twenty-four hours is operationally achievable for a security team of our size.

Bramber provides reasonable assistance with data protection impact assessments and prior consultations, including the information in the DPA, the security schedule and the transfer assessment. Assistance that requires significant engineering or legal work is charged at standard rates.
A completed pre-assessment questionnaire and a standard DPIA pack, with bespoke assistance charged at cost and subject to a written scope.
An open-ended obligation to assist with any DPIA the customer chooses to conduct, or a requirement to participate in regulatory consultations without a defined scope.

A DPIA is the controller's obligation. We can supply the facts about our processing, but we cannot assess the customer's purpose, necessity or proportionality. An open-ended assistance clause converts a legal duty into an unbounded professional services commitment.

The customer may audit Bramber's compliance once in any 12-month period, on at least 30 days' written notice, during business hours and remotely where possible. The auditor is independent, bound by confidentiality and has no access to other customers' data. The customer bears the cost unless the audit reveals a material discrepancy.
Twice in any 12-month period for regulated customers, with 15 Business Days' notice, a maximum of five auditor days per audit and costs shared where the audit is inconclusive.
Audits on less than 5 Business Days' notice, unlimited frequency, access to production systems or sub-processor premises, or audits at Bramber's cost regardless of outcome.
Elena Marchetti, DPO. Jonas Reed, CISO for notice of less than 15 Business Days.

Audit rights are the most frequently over-drafted part of a DPA. The customer rarely needs a physical inspection; it needs evidence that the controls operate. Remote audits, certifications and a defined scope give the same assurance at a fraction of the operational cost.

On termination, Bramber returns customer data in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, then deletes it within 30 days, unless retention is required by law. A certificate of deletion is available on request. Backup copies are deleted in accordance with the backup rotation.
Deletion within 90 days to align with the backup cycle, with a certificate of deletion and a retention carve-out for statutory records.
Immediate deletion of backups, an obligation to retain data indefinitely, or a right for the customer to audit deletion by accessing Bramber's infrastructure.

Deletion is constrained by the backup architecture. Promising immediate deletion of every copy is a promise we cannot keep and a misrepresentation risk. A 30-day primary deletion plus a documented backup rotation is the honest position.

Liability under the DPA is subject to the limitations in the MSA. Each party is responsible for its own regulatory fines. Bramber indemnifies the customer for third-party claims caused by Bramber's breach of the DPA, subject to the cap. The DPA continues for as long as Bramber processes personal data.
A separate data protection super-cap of 2x the annual fee, with fines allocated according to responsibility and a mutual obligation to mitigate.
An uncapped indemnity for all fines, penalties and compensation, or an obligation to indemnify the customer for the customer's own acts and omissions.
Elena Marchetti, DPO. Priya Raghavan, GC and Marcus Feld, CFO for any uncapped liability or indemnity.

A regulatory fine is the consequence of a breach of law, not a debt that can be allocated by contract. An uncapped indemnity for fines is uninsurable and would expose the company to a liability larger than its balance sheet. The MSA cap is the only defensible allocation for a business of our size.

data.title: DP-01  Roles and scope
data.contentText: DP-01 | DPA | Bramber is a processor and the customer is a controller. The DPA describes the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, the categories of personal data and the categories of data subjects in a schedule. Bramber does not determine the purposes or means of processing. | Bramber is a processor for customer data and an independent controller for account, billing and service telemetry data. The DPA must identify the controller data separately and limit the processor obligations to the customer data. | Any description of Bramber as a controller or joint controller of customer data, or any obligation to determine the lawful basis for the customer's processing. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. Priya Raghavan, GC for any controller or joint-controller language. | Role allocation is the foundation of the DPA. A processor acts on instructions; a controller decides why and how data is processed. Accepting controller language would make Bramber responsible for the customer's lawful basis, notices and retention decisions, which we cannot verify and do not control.

data.title: DP-12  Liability, indemnity and term
data.contentText: DP-12 | DPA | Liability under the DPA is subject to the limitations in the MSA. Each party is responsible for its own regulatory fines. Bramber indemnifies the customer for third-party claims caused by Bramber's breach of the DPA, subject to the cap. The DPA continues for as long as Bramber processes personal data. | A separate data protection super-cap of 2x the annual fee, with fines allocated according to responsibility and a mutual obligation to mitigate. | An uncapped indemnity for all fines, penalties and compensation, or an obligation to indemnify the customer for the customer's own acts and omissions. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. Priya Raghavan, GC and Marcus Feld, CFO for any uncapped liability or indemnity. | A regulatory fine is the consequence of a breach of law, not a debt that can be allocated by contract. An uncapped indemnity for fines is uninsurable and would expose the company to a liability larger than its balance sheet. The MSA cap is the only defensible allocation for a business of our size.

data.title: DP-08  Personal data breach notification
data.contentText: DP-08 | DPA | Bramber notifies the customer without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach affecting customer data. The notice includes the nature of the breach, the data and individuals affected, likely consequences and measures taken or proposed. | Notification within 72 hours of awareness, with an initial notice followed by a fuller report within 5 Business Days. A 72-hour period is the regulatory outer limit for the controller, not a target for the processor. | Notification within 5 Business Days or more, a requirement to notify the regulator directly on the customer's behalf, or an obligation to indemnify the customer for all regulatory fines. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. Jonas Reed, CISO for any change to the notification period. | The controller's 72-hour clock starts when it becomes aware, which is usually when we tell it. A processor notification period that consumes the whole 72 hours leaves the customer unable to comply. Twenty-four hours is operationally achievable for a security team of our size.

data.title: DP-03  Confidentiality of personnel
data.contentText: DP-03 | DPA | Personnel authorised to process personal data are bound by confidentiality obligations, have received appropriate training, and have access only on a need-to-know basis. Confidentiality survives termination of employment. | Confidentiality obligations in employment contracts plus annual privacy training, with evidence available on request rather than a separate undertaking for each engagement. | A requirement to name every individual with access, or to obtain customer approval for individual staff members. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. | Access control is an operational security measure, not a contractual permission slip. Naming individuals creates a maintenance burden and a privacy issue of its own; the customer needs assurance about the control, not the names.

data.title: DP-05  Sub-processors

payloadColumns.Approver: Elena Marchetti, DPO. Tom Whitlock, Senior Commercial Counsel for any consent right beyond general authorisation.
payloadColumns.Fallback: Prior written consent for new sub-processors, not unreasonably withheld or delayed, with deemed approval after 10 Business Days and a right to use affiliates without consent.
payloadColumns.Rationale: Our platform runs on hyperscale infrastructure and a small number of specialist services. A veto right over sub-processors is a veto over our ability to operate and scale. General authorisation with notice and objection is the model the EDPB guidelines contemplate for stable processing chains.
payloadColumns.Walk-away: Absolute consent for each sub-processor, a veto over cloud infrastructure providers, or a requirement that Bramber's affiliates be treated as third parties requiring consent.

data.title: DP-10  Audit and inspection
data.contentText: DP-10 | DPA | The customer may audit Bramber's compliance once in any 12-month period, on at least 30 days' written notice, during business hours and remotely where possible. The auditor is independent, bound by confidentiality and has no access to other customers' data. The customer bears the cost unless the audit reveals a material discrepancy. | Twice in any 12-month period for regulated customers, with 15 Business Days' notice, a maximum of five auditor days per audit and costs shared where the audit is inconclusive. | Audits on less than 5 Business Days' notice, unlimited frequency, access to production systems or sub-processor premises, or audits at Bramber's cost regardless of outcome. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. Jonas Reed, CISO for notice of less than 15 Business Days. | Audit rights are the most frequently over-drafted part of a DPA. The customer rarely needs a physical inspection; it needs evidence that the controls operate. Remote audits, certifications and a defined scope give the same assurance at a fraction of the operational cost.

data.title: DP-04  Security measures
data.contentText: DP-04 | DPA | The technical and organisational measures in the security schedule are appropriate to the risk and include encryption in transit and at rest, role-based access, logging and monitoring, vulnerability management, secure development, business continuity and incident response. data.title: DP-11  Return and deletion
data.contentText: DP-11 | DPA | On termination, Bramber returns customer data in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, then deletes it within 30 days, unless retention is required by law. A certificate of deletion is available on request. Backup copies are deleted in accordance with the backup rotation. | Deletion within 90 days to align with the backup cycle, with a certificate of deletion and a retention carve-out for statutory records. | Immediate deletion of backups, an obligation to retain data indefinitely, or a right for the customer to audit deletion by accessing Bramber's infrastructure. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. | Deletion is constrained by the backup architecture. Promising immediate deletion of every copy is a promise we cannot keep and a misrepresentation risk. A 30-day primary deletion plus a documented backup rotation is the honest position.

payloadColumns.Fallback: Deletion within 90 days to align with the backup cycle, with a certificate of deletion and a retention carve-out for statutory records.
payloadColumns.Rationale: Deletion is constrained by the backup architecture. Promising immediate deletion of every copy is a promise we cannot keep and a misrepresentation risk. A 30-day primary deletion plus a documented backup rotation is the honest position.
payloadColumns.Walk-away: Immediate deletion of backups, an obligation to retain data indefinitely, or a right for the customer to audit deletion by accessing Bramber's infrastructure.

data.title: DP-07  Data subject rights
data.contentText: DP-07 | DPA | Bramber assists the customer with data subject requests by appropriate technical and organisational measures, taking into account the nature of the processing. Assistance is provided within the customer's response window where feasible, and Bramber does not respond to requests directly unless instructed. | Assistance through the self-service tools in the platform, with bespoke support charged at standard professional services rates where the request requires manual work. | An obligation to respond directly to data subjects on the customer's behalf, or to guarantee a response within a period shorter than the platform's deletion and export cycles allow. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. | The customer owns the relationship with the data subject. Our obligation is to give them the tools and information they need, not to become the controller's front office. A direct-response obligation also creates a risk of conflicting instructions from different customers.

payloadColumns.Walk-away: An obligation to respond directly to data subjects on the customer's behalf, or to guarantee a response within a period shorter than the platform's deletion and export cycles allow.

data.title: DP-02  Processing instructions
data.contentText: DP-02 | DPA | Bramber processes personal data only on the customer's documented instructions, including for transfers, unless required by law. If a law requires processing, Bramber informs the customer before processing unless prohibited from doing so. The DPA and the order form together constitute the instructions. | A general instruction to provide the services in accordance with the documentation, with a change-control process for new instructions and a right to charge for instruction changes. | An obligation to comply with instructions that are unlawful, or a right for the customer to instruct processing outside the scope of the services without a change order. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. | The instruction set is what separates a processor from a controller in practice. It also gives Bramber a defensible position if a customer asks for processing that is outside the documented service or unlawful in the destination country.

data.title: DP-06  International transfers
data.contentText: DP-06 | DPA | Transfers outside the UK or EEA are covered by the UK International Data Transfer Addendum, the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (Module 2) or an adequacy decision, together with a transfer risk assessment. The mechanism is named in the DPA and matches the destination. | The customer's preferred transfer mechanism where it is legally valid and the destination has been assessed. A supplementary measures schedule may be required for US transfers. | Transfers to a country without a valid mechanism, a representation that the destination is adequate when it is not, or an obligation to use a mechanism the customer has not executed. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. | A transfer clause is only as good as the mechanism behind it. The UK Addendum and the EU SCCs are the two mechanisms our customers most often require; naming the wrong one creates a gap that a regulator will find before we do.

data.title: DP-01  Roles and scope
data.contentText: DP-01 | DPA | Bramber is a processor and the customer is a controller. The DPA describes the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, the categories of personal data and the categories of data subjects in a schedule. Bramber does not determine the purposes or means of processing. | Bramber is a processor for customer data and an independent controller for account, billing and service telemetry data. The DPA must identify the controller data separately and limit the processor obligations to the customer data. | Any description of Bramber as a controller or joint controller of customer data, or any obligation to determine the lawful basis for the customer's processing. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. Priya Raghavan, GC for any controller or joint-controller language. | Role allocation is the foundation of the DPA. A processor acts on instructions; a controller decides why and how data is processed. Accepting controller language would make Bramber responsible for the customer's lawful basis, notices and retention decisions, which we cannot verify and do not control.

data.title: DP-12  Liability, indemnity and term
data.contentText: DP-12 | DPA | Liability under the DPA is subject to the limitations in the MSA. Each party is responsible for its own regulatory fines. Bramber indemnifies the customer for third-party claims caused by Bramber's breach of the DPA, subject to the cap. The DPA continues for as long as Bramber processes personal data. | A separate data protection super-cap of 2x the annual fee, with fines allocated according to responsibility and a mutual obligation to mitigate. | An uncapped indemnity for all fines, penalties and compensation, or an obligation to indemnify the customer for the customer's own acts and omissions. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. Priya Raghavan, GC and Marcus Feld, CFO for any uncapped liability or indemnity. | A regulatory fine is the consequence of a breach of law, not a debt that can be allocated by contract. An uncapped indemnity for fines is uninsurable and would expose the company to a liability larger than its balance sheet. The MSA cap is the only defensible allocation for a business of our size.

data.title: DP-08  Personal data breach notification
data.contentText: DP-08 | DPA | Bramber notifies the customer without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach affecting customer data. The notice includes the nature of the breach, the data and individuals affected, likely consequences and measures taken or proposed. | Notification within 72 hours of awareness, with an initial notice followed by a fuller report within 5 Business Days. A 72-hour period is the regulatory outer limit for the controller, not a target for the processor. | Notification within 5 Business Days or more, a requirement to notify the regulator directly on the customer's behalf, or an obligation to indemnify the customer for all regulatory fines. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. Jonas Reed, CISO for any change to the notification period. | The controller's 72-hour clock starts when it becomes aware, which is usually when we tell it. A processor notification period that consumes the whole 72 hours leaves the customer unable to comply. Twenty-four hours is operationally achievable for a security team of our size.

data.title: DP-03  Confidentiality of personnel
data.contentText: DP-03 | DPA | Personnel authorised to process personal data are bound by confidentiality obligations, have received appropriate training, and have access only on a need-to-know basis. Confidentiality survives termination of employment. | Confidentiality obligations in employment contracts plus annual privacy training, with evidence available on request rather than a separate undertaking for each engagement. | A requirement to name every individual with access, or to obtain customer approval for individual staff members. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. | Access control is an operational security measure, not a contractual permission slip. Naming individuals creates a maintenance burden and a privacy issue of its own; the customer needs assurance about the control, not the names.

payloadColumns.Fallback: Confidentiality obligations in employment contracts plus annual privacy training, with evidence available on request rather than a separate undertaking for each engagement.
payloadColumns.Rationale: Access control is an operational security measure, not a contractual permission slip. Naming individuals creates a maintenance burden and a privacy issue of its own; the customer needs assurance about the control, not the names.
payloadColumns.Walk-away: A requirement to name every individual with access, or to obtain customer approval for individual staff members.
payloadColumns.Our position: Personnel authorised to process personal data are bound by confidentiality obligations, have received appropriate training, and have access only on a need-to-know basis. Confidentiality survives termination of employment.

data.title: DP-05  Sub-processors

payloadColumns.Approver: Elena Marchetti, DPO. Tom Whitlock, Senior Commercial Counsel for any consent right beyond general authorisation.
payloadColumns.Fallback: Prior written consent for new sub-processors, not unreasonably withheld or delayed, with deemed approval after 10 Business Days and a right to use affiliates without consent.
payloadColumns.Rationale: Our platform runs on hyperscale infrastructure and a small number of specialist services. A veto right over sub-processors is a veto over our ability to operate and scale. General authorisation with notice and objection is the model the EDPB guidelines contemplate for stable processing chains.
payloadColumns.Walk-away: Absolute consent for each sub-processor, a veto over cloud infrastructure providers, or a requirement that Bramber's affiliates be treated as third parties requiring consent.

data.escalationTrigger: Elena Marchetti, DPO. Tom Whitlock, Senior Commercial Counsel for any consent right beyond general authorisation.
data.preferredText: The customer gives general written authorisation for sub-processors. Bramber maintains a current list in the DPA, notifies changes at least 30 days in advance, and gives the customer a right to object on reasonable data protection grounds. Bramber remains liable for its sub-processors' performance. The sub-processor list in the DPA shall state, for each sub-processor: its legal name and registered address; the processing it performs and the categories of personal data concerned; the country of processing and the transfer mechanism, where applicable.

data.title: DP-10  Audit and inspection
data.contentText: DP-10 | DPA | The customer may audit Bramber's compliance once in any 12-month period, on at least 30 days' written notice, during business hours and remotely where possible. The auditor is independent, bound by confidentiality and has no access to other customers' data. The customer bears the cost unless the audit reveals a material discrepancy. | Twice in any 12-month period for regulated customers, with 15 Business Days' notice, a maximum of five auditor days per audit and costs shared where the audit is inconclusive. | Audits on less than 5 Business Days' notice, unlimited frequency, access to production systems or sub-processor premises, or audits at Bramber's cost regardless of outcome. | Elena Marchetti, DPO. Jonas Reed, CISO for notice of less than 15 Business Days. | Audit rights are the most frequently over-drafted part of a DPA. The customer rarely needs a physical inspection; it needs evidence that the controls operate. Remote audits, certifications and a defined scope give the same assurance at a fraction of the operational cost.
